summary: Specifies a pulse-per-second API for UNIX-like systems, because earlier work left implementors without a portable way to use PPS sources, which are precise timing signals. This is an informational memo.

plainLanguage.summary: A clock sends a tick every second. This defines a standard way for programs to listen to those ticks.

questions: how to use pulse per second on unix
how does ntp use pps signals
which systems support the pps api
subtitle: A standard interface for precise timing signals in UNIX systems.

tldr.problem: UNIX systems needed a way to use high-accuracy pulse-per-second signals from time sources like GPS receivers, but RFC 1589 did not define how application programs could access these signals.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC specifies a C API with functions to obtain PPS source handles, configure capture modes, retrieve timestamped events, and bind PPS signals to the kernel's timebase for synchronization.
tldr.outcome: Applications and UNIX kernels can now use precise one-second timing pulses in a portable, standardized way, enabling accurate time synchronization without relying on general-purpose operating system timing.

today: RFC 2783 is an Informational RFC that remains the standard specification for PPS APIs on UNIX-like systems. It has not been obsoleted, and implementations exist on Linux, FreeBSD, Solaris and other systems.

sections.title: Introduction and Motivation
sections.content:
RFC 1589 introduced a kernel model for high-precision timekeeping on UNIX systems that could work with the Network Time Protocol (NTP). One key part of this model is support for pulse-per-second (PPS) signals, which are periodic timing pulses from external sources like GPS or GOES receivers. These signals are far more accurate than the system's internal clock.

However, RFC 1589 never defined an application programming interface (API)—the set of functions and data structures that application code uses to access the PPS facility. This left implementors without a standard way to use PPS sources across different UNIX systems and compilers. RFC 2783 fills that gap by specifying a portable PPS API.
sections.plainLanguage: Big buildings have atomic clocks that know what time it is very precisely. GPS receivers can listen to these clocks and send a signal every second. But there was no standard way for UNIX programs to use these signals, so this RFC writes down how to do it.

sections.title: The Pulse-Per-Second Signal
sections.content:
A PPS signal is a periodic electrical pulse, typically one pulse per second. Each pulse has an asserted phase (logical true, a high voltage) and a clear phase (logical false, a low voltage). The API can capture a timestamp at the moment the signal transitions into the asserted phase, and optionally another timestamp at the transition into the clear phase.

The RFC does not define which physical voltage levels mean true or false—that depends on the hardware interface (TTL, RS-232C, etc.). A typical setup connects the PPS signal to a modem-control pin on a serial line, such as the Data Carrier Detect (DCD) pin. When the transition happens, the operating system receives an interrupt and records a timestamp as soon as possible.
sections.plainLanguage: Imagine flipping a light switch on and off once every second. The computer can take a snapshot of the exact time when it flips, faster than its regular timer can.

sections.title: Data Structures and Mode Bits
sections.content:
The API defines several key data structures. A pps_handle_t is an opaque identifier representing one PPS source. The pps_info_t structure holds timestamps captured from a PPS source, including the timestamp and sequence number for both assert and clear events, plus mode bits indicating which formats are active.

The pps_params_t structure holds configuration parameters: an API version number, mode bits that control capture behavior, and optional offset values to correct for cable delays. Mode bits fall into three categories: device parameters (which edges to capture), kernel actions (echo signals, offset application), and timestamp formats (the RFC supports both POSIX timespec and NTP fixed-point formats).
sections.plainLanguage: The computer needs to remember which PPS signal you're listening to, what time it saw, and how you want to receive the time (in seconds-and-nanoseconds or in another format).

sections.title: The API Functions
sections.content:
The RFC defines six required functions. time_pps_create() turns an open file descriptor into a PPS handle; time_pps_destroy() releases it. time_pps_getparams() and time_pps_setparams() read and write configuration (mode bits, offsets). time_pps_getcap() reports which capabilities the device supports without generating an error. time_pps_fetch() retrieves the most recent timestamps, with optional blocking until the next timestamp arrives.

The RFC also defines one optional function, time_pps_kcbind(), which binds a kernel consumer (such as the hardpps() function for disciplining the timebase) to a PPS source. This lets the kernel directly adjust the system clock based on PPS events, without waiting for application code to do it.
sections.plainLanguage: You open a serial line, ask the system to watch it for PPS pulses, ask what settings it supports, and then either loop reading timestamps or let the kernel use the pulses automatically to set the clock.

sections.title: Compliance and Use Cases
sections.content:
The RFC specifies that all implementations MUST support the core functions and at least one capture mode (assert or clear, or both). All implementations MUST support the POSIX timespec timestamp format. Support for NTP fixed-point format, echo signals, offset correction, and blocking fetch operations is OPTIONAL.

In practice, the API is used in two ways. User-level time-synchronization software (like NTP daemons) calls time_pps_fetch() to read timestamped PPS events and compare them to the time code received on the same serial line, determining the system clock's offset. Alternatively, the kernel can be told to directly discipline the system clock from PPS events via time_pps_kcbind(), providing precise timing to all applications without per-application code.
sections.plainLanguage: Programs can read the pulses themselves, or they can tell the kernel to adjust the system clock from the pulses, so all programs on the computer automatically use the correct time.
